text.p: New York State Electric & Gas Corp said Wednesday it has reached an agreement with the New York Public Service Commission Staff on the principles to govern a settlement of the utility's restructuring proceeding.
Among other things, the company said, it would forego previously approved rate increases totaling six percent that were scheduled to become effective in August of 1996 and 1997.
Participants in NYSEG's talks with the staff and other interested parties said it was the utility's demand that it get the 1996 increase that put the case into litigation.
In addition to foregoing the approved residential and commercial rate increases, NYSEG said, the agreement freezes these prices through July 31, 2002.
Rates for large-use industrial and commercial customers would be reduced by five percent each year for the next five years, it said.

In addition, the utility said, there is the potential to reduce prices another nine percent, since the company intends to pass back to customers savings from renegotiation of non-utility generator contracts and the passage of securitization legislation.

Furthermore, if the legislature approved the replacement of the gross receipts tax with a "profits-based tax," electric prices could be reduced another 3.1 percent. The combined effect of all these actions would be a reduction in average electric prices of about 20 percent from previously authorized levels, it said.

According to the agreement, NYSEG said in a statement, "The settlement meets all of the PSC's rate goals. It encourages economic development and freezes prices under a hard five-year price cap. The aggregate value of the revenue concessions is nearly $600 million."
The utility said the agreement would govern a settlement of its proceeding to establish the terms on which competition will be promoted in its service territory.

"This is an important milestone in our transition to competition. It presents the most aggressive plan in the state for implementing 'customer choice' and reinforces our commitment to competition," chief executive Wes von Schack said.

Later he told Reuters "This is something that we have been working on for some time. We have been working with the Public Service Commission for months, totally independent of CalEnergy's (Co Inc's acquisition) bid."
"It is an extemely comeprehensive, complex agreement that we finally finished off," he said in a telephone interview.

However, the company's statement gave few details on how the settlement would restructure the company for competition. And commission spokesman Ed Collins said nothing has been filed with the commission. He said a filing is expected later Wednesday.

NYSEG's statement did say a retail choice program would proceed, under which all customers would be permitted to buy electricity in a competitive marketplace by August 1, 1999; and the company would separate its fossil fuel generation into an unregulated subsidiary.
It said the fossil generating units would be subject to an auction process in which the company could participate. Value achieved from the auction process would also benefit customers.
It also said the agreement would extend the current natural gas settlement through July 31, 2002, adding this would freeze prices.
NYSEG said "The real price of electricity could be reduced by 35 percent over the next five years when inflation is factored into our plans."
